tldr: SMARTS is an open-source scalable multi-agent RL training platform for autonomous driving that supports realistic, diverse multi-agent interactions through a bootstrapping Social Agent Zoo and a novel bubble mechanism for scenario composition.
contributions: Introduction of SMARTS, an industrial-strength open-source simulation platform for MARL research in autonomous driving
Social Agent Zoo with a bootstrapping strategy for growing diverse and realistic behavior models of road users
Bubble mechanism enabling spatiotemporal handover of social vehicle control from background traffic to learned social agents
Comprehensive MARL benchmarking suite with AD-specific evaluation metrics covering model performance, agent population behavior, and game-theoretic analysis
Integration with multiple RL libraries (RLlib, PyMARL, MAlib) and implementations of MARL algorithms across all paradigms including CTDE
methods: SMARTS uses a provider-based compositional architecture with three main providers: a background traffic provider (SUMO), a vehicle physics provider (Bullet-based), and a motion plan provider. Scenarios are composed using a Python-based domain-specific language (DSL) and 'bubbles'—spatiotemporal regions where social agents from the Social Agent Zoo take control of vehicles for interactive maneuvers. The Social Agent Zoo grows iteratively through self-play and population-based training, grounded by real-world driving data. Distributed computing is supported through Ray, allowing social agents to run in separate processes, potentially on remote machines, with flexible framework dependencies (TensorFlow/PyTorch). The platform provides configurable observation spaces (dynamic object lists, BEV grids, RGB images, ego states), four controller types, and integrates with RLlib, PyMARL, and MAlib.
results: Experiments were conducted using seven MARL algorithms across three increasingly challenging interactive scenarios: Two-Way traffic, Double Merge, and Unprotected Intersection. The paper demonstrates that SMARTS can train ego agents in scenarios requiring non-trivial interactive capabilities. A comprehensive set of MARL algorithms was implemented, described as the most comprehensive set to their knowledge covering all MARL paradigms including centralized training & decentralized execution (CTDE) and networked agent learning. limitations: Existing AD research has mostly focused on M0 (rule-based) with limited attempts at M1 and M2, indicating the field is early-stage for advanced multi-agent learning
No existing open-source simulator adequately addresses the specific need for in-depth MARL research on autonomous driving interaction
Prior efforts like highway-env and BARK are limited in either scenario diversity or multi-agent research support
Ray's MARL support is noted as highly limited since it focuses mainly on single-agent RL
Current evaluation metrics in AD tend to focus only on macro driving performance without explaining why agents achieve certain performance levels
